intro: Apply the preceding concepts to a business decision. AI has combined three department sheets into sales.xlsx. This step calculates a total and saves monthly_sales.xlsx. The example covers this step, not the full merge.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: example scope and business purpose
overview.lead: Further reading: a summary file has been generated and will be used for customer sales rankings. Switch between three records to see how technical results affect business decisions.

paragraphs: Rows without customer names affect a departmental total differently from a customer ranking. Execution status describes program completion; the intended use determines what still needs checking.
The three situations below show a warning, no printed text, and a read failure. Inspect code and both channels, choose a conclusion, then read its reasoning and a useful follow-up request.
sections.title: The same result can matter differently for different uses

intro: First identify the inputs, processing, and destination of results. Then compare those actions with your requirements. You can learn common syntax gradually without first mastering the entire language.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: conditions, loops, indentation, and business rules

facts.text: print creates a text record. Saving a file requires a write operation.
facts.title: Printing ≠ saving a file

facts.text: Finishing the code does not prove it used the right file, column, or business rule.
facts.title: Check even after a normal return

overview.lead: Identify the input, processing steps, and result, then check them against your request. These three lines introduce variables, functions, and printing.

paragraphs: Quoted content is usually text, such as a file name, column name, or message. Read operations select inputs; calculations, filters, and conversions process them; saving, returning, or printing sends results somewhere.
print(...) commonly writes text; it does not automatically create a spreadsheet. read_excel(...) and to_excel(...) commonly read and save spreadsheets through a package.
sections.title: Find inputs, processing, and results

paragraphs: A variable names data in a program. items = [10, 20, 30] stores three numbers under the name items; = means assignment here. Later instructions can use that name.

A function is an operation you can call. sum(items) adds the numbers; parentheses call the function, and items is a parameter telling it what to process. The result can be stored under another name, total.
sections.title: Recognize variables, functions, and parameters

paragraphs: if selects actions when a condition holds; for commonly repeats actions for each item; import introduces a package. Python uses indentation to define which statements belong to a condition or loop.
Only the indented print below repeats for each number. The final statement is outside the loop and runs once. Follow these structures to understand longer scripts.
sections.title: Conditions, loops, and indentation matter

paragraphs: A normally completed program may still use the wrong file or column, or omit a filter. Your business knowledge remains necessary. Ask AI to explain inputs, steps, and outputs in plain language and compare record counts or totals.
sections.title: Compare business requirements with written rules

intro: A failed execution encountered a problem that prevented it from continuing: a missing file, invalid format, misspelled name, or unavailable dependency, for example. This is feedback for AI to investigate; it does not by itself mean the whole task failed.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: Traceback, another attempt, and completed actions

facts.text: While AI investigates or revises, watch the next record. Step in when information is needed or attempts make no progress.
facts.title: Watch what happens next

facts.text: Failure does not undo previous writes. Another execution must consider repeated work and overwriting.
facts.title: Earlier changes may remain

overview.lead: This execution stopped, and its error is returned to AI. AI can investigate and revise the script for another attempt. One failed card does not establish that the whole task has failed.

paragraphs: The tool returns error information to AI. AI can inspect inputs and the environment, revise the script, or use another approach. When a card shows failure, first check whether AI is still working and what later attempts produce.

Each card keeps that execution’s record; a later success does not rewrite an earlier failure. Assess the task using later valid results, artifacts, and AI’s final explanation. Automatic retries cannot resolve every problem.
sections.title: What does AI do next?

paragraphs: Python errors often start with Traceback, which records the calls leading to the problem. The last line commonly gives the error type and reason; file names and line numbers locate the relevant code. Start with the cause, then find your script.

In the example below, NameError means a name was used without being defined. The script defines total but writes totla on line 3. It stops while printing; AI can correct the spelling and execute again.
sections.title: How do you read an error?

paragraphs: Unhandled exceptions stop the script, but earlier file writes may already have occurred. Before retrying, AI needs to consider repeated processing or overwriting artifacts. You can state which original data should be preserved.

If AI is investigating and revising, continue observing. If it requests information, permission, or a business decision, or repeatedly makes no progress, your involvement is needed. The next chapter explains these cases.
sections.title: Earlier actions may already have happened

intro: An execution has three stages: prepare the code, run the instructions, and return the results to AI. They distinguish AI reasoning, program execution, and reading an execution record.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: execution order, runtime, and the whole task

facts.text: A task may include several executions. Earlier cards retain their original results.
facts.title: One card, one execution

facts.text: Text appears in the output tabs. Generated files are checked in project files.
facts.title: Text and files

overview.lead: AI sends code to an execution tool, which starts Python in the runtime. The result returns to AI so it can decide what to do next.

paragraphs: Execution takes place in the platform’s environment. A tool starts Python, passes in the code, and collects text and completion status. The browser detail panel displays the record.
The script may read workspace files, use installed packages, and save new files. Text appears in the output tabs; generated files are separate artifacts to inspect in Project files.
sections.title: Displaying code does not execute it

paragraphs: Ordinary statements generally run from top to bottom. Conditions select actions, loops repeat them, and functions group actions for reuse.
An unhandled error stops the execution before later instructions. Earlier operations may already have taken effect; failure does not mean nothing happened.
sections.title: Instructions follow the program’s structure

paragraphs: AI may run one script to inspect inputs, another to process them, and another to verify results. Each has its own record. A card describes one execution.
Results return to AI’s context so it can continue, revise the code, or request information. AI can adapt to errors, but success still depends on the inputs, environment, and approach.
sections.title: One execution within a larger task

intro: AI can handle many execution details, but it does not know business facts you have not supplied and cannot make every authorization or decision for you. Your involvement supplies evidence, makes decisions, or stops an unsuitable action.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: information, evidence, and stopping work
overview.lead: You provide business decisions and missing information; AI handles further technical work. Whether to step in depends on what it currently needs.

paragraphs: Checks of paths or files, changes of approach, and new execution cards indicate continued work. One error can be part of that process. Read later attempts and the final explanation instead of requesting a restart after every failed card.
sections.title: Wait while AI is investigating and revising

paragraphs: Missing files, wrong attachments, or incomplete information require correct inputs from you. Account sign-in or an explicit authorization may require your action or decision.
Specify duplicate rules, accounting definitions, refund handling, and authoritative data sources. Ask AI to list uncertainties and confirm them before processing.
sections.title: Supply missing information, permission, or business rules

paragraphs: If AI has stopped with an incomplete task, ask it to continue and identify the missing result. If the same problem recurs, request the checks already made, evidence, and the next action rather than an unchanged retry.
Name the file, failed step, key message, and intended outcome. For example: identify the file being read, explain why its format cannot be recognized, and choose a fix based on the checks.
sections.title: Ask for evidence when work stops or repeats without progress

paragraphs: If AI is using the wrong input, misunderstood the task, or is about to overwrite or delete something you want to preserve, stop the current processing in the conversation input area and provide a correction.
Stopping does not necessarily undo completed file operations. Before continuing, ask which actions already occurred and which artifacts remain.
sections.title: Stop promptly if the direction is wrong

intro: Python is a programming language for describing calculations, file operations, and data processing as instructions a computer can execute. Its syntax specifies how a program handles its input and produces results.
A script is a program written to perform an operation. It can be saved in a .py file or executed as a temporary code snippet. Here, AI writes Python for your request and uses a tool to run it.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: packages, read-only cards, and execution records

facts.text: Python defines the syntax; a script specifies the work for this execution.
facts.title: Language and script

facts.text: AI writes and revises instructions. Python processes data as instructed.
facts.title: AI and execution

overview.lead: Python is a programming language. A script is a set of instructions written in that language; AI can use it to read files, calculate, or organize data.

paragraphs: Python is the language; the script contains specific instructions; AI understands the request and writes or changes those instructions. The Python interpreter in the execution environment actually executes them.
AI may decide which data to calculate, while Python follows the written read, calculate, and save instructions. The code and execution records let you inspect the inputs and actions.
sections.title: What do Python, a script, and AI each do?

paragraphs: Computers handle repeated, explicitly defined operations well, such as processing many rows, converting formats, or organizing files. A script records repeatable steps that can be checked.

Python can also use existing packages for drawing charts or reading documents. A package is a collection of capabilities written by others; importing it makes those capabilities available to the script.
sections.title: Why does AI use scripts?

paragraphs: The code area shows the script for this execution. Standard output and Standard error show text emitted by the program. The return status and exit code describe how this execution ended.
The code is read-only. Reading, copying, searching, or switching tabs does not execute it. Ask AI in the conversation when you need a change or another execution.
sections.title: What does this detail card contain?

intro: Search, word wrap, end navigation, and height adjustment help with long output. They change how you read; they do not change the script or data or execute it again.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: search scope, wrapping, and reading space

facts.text: Select standard error to search diagnostics. A missing match may mean the script never printed that information.
facts.title: Search the selected channel

facts.text: If a record says content was omitted or truncated, investigate further. The visible window is not all the data.
facts.title: Check completeness

overview.lead: These tools change how you read the output. They do not change data or execute the script again. Try them in the output panel below.

paragraphs: Search output displays match counts. The up/down arrows move between matches. Search applies to the selected channel; switch to Standard error to find diagnostics.
sections.title: Search and switch channels

paragraphs: Jump to end shows the final records. Word wrap fits long text within the available width without adding line breaks to the original output.

Only part of a long record fits on screen. Not finding a business item does not prove it is absent from the data; it may never have been printed. Explicit omission or truncation notices define completeness.
sections.title: Jump to end and word wrap

paragraphs: Expand or collapse code using the top control. Drag the divider or use keyboard arrows to adjust proportions. Expand code to inspect processing steps and give results more room for long records.
sections.title: Allocate space between code and results

intro: Programs have two default text output channels: standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr). They carry two types of information from one execution. Switching tabs does not execute a different script.

overview.detailsTitle: Read more: channel conventions, empty output, and exit codes

facts.text: Gray: no text. Neither color reports task success or failure.
facts.title: Blue: text is available

facts.text: 0 usually means a normal exit; other codes usually indicate an abnormal exit.
facts.title: Exit code: how it ended

overview.lead: Programs have two text output channels. Standard output usually contains results; standard error usually contains warnings and diagnostics. A channel name does not tell you whether execution succeeded.

paragraphs: This usually carries results, progress, or statistics. Python print(...) writes here by default. The messages depend on what the script prints.
An execution can calculate or save without printing anything. To verify a generated file, inspect the save operation and actual artifact.
sections.title: Standard output: ordinary program messages

paragraphs: This usually carries warnings, diagnostics, and unhandled exceptions. Its name describes a channel convention; text there does not necessarily mean failure. Packages may also report warnings or progress there.
A program may finish normally while warning that optional information is missing. Read the message and the top return status together.
sections.title: Standard error: a diagnostic channel

paragraphs: Has output and No output only indicate whether that channel has text. Blue means text is available; grey means it is empty. The top return status and exit code describe how execution ended.

A normal return usually corresponds to exit code 0; other codes typically indicate abnormal completion. Normal execution still requires checking business correctness. The channels are collected separately, so their tab positions do not establish message timing.
sections.title: What do badges, colors, and status mean?

content.actionContinue: Usually, continue the same task and let the system handle earlier content. “Organize now” lets you organize earlier, but is not an automatic organization switch.
content.actionMaterials: Give AI a clear goal, necessary materials and file locations instead of pasting the same long content repeatedly. For exact data, ask it to read the corresponding file rather than recall it only from a summary.
content.actionTitle: 5. What should I do when usage is high?
content.actionTopic: For an independent new task, create a topic with the necessary background. A new topic and context organization serve different purposes; there is no need to switch repeatedly to chase a lower number.
content.autoIntro: You do not need to watch the usage or click “Organize now” to continue. The system summarizes earlier content to make room for the rest of the conversation.
content.autoLead: When the conversation is almost full, the system organizes it automatically. You do not need to do anything.
content.budgetTitle: Read usage and the organization threshold together
content.exampleCaption: Example: 122K / 200K = 61%. Input text is approximately 120K, including 12K of skill instructions and 24K of MCP output. Colors show an approximate text composition; total usage comes from the model.
content.filesKept: Automatic organization does not delete generated files or undo completed actions. You can still use earlier reports, tables and other results.
content.filesNote: Storing a file in the project does not mean its full contents enter every request. Only content actually prepared for this answer belongs to this request’s input.
content.filesReread: What changes is the conversation content AI refers to next: a summary replaces earlier long discussions. To check file details again, tell AI the file name and what to check so it can reread the material.
content.filesTitle: 3. Will my files or completed work disappear?
content.historyLimits: Chat history helps check what was discussed; original files help check what the material actually says. History lookup relies on records that remain accessible. It does not guarantee permanent storage or recovery of every detail. Keep important materials and lasting requirements in files or long-term memory.
content.inputsLessonDescription: AI uses more than the messages you see. The system also supplies working rules, available tool descriptions, materials already read and tool results for the task.
content.inputsLessonGrowth: Usage can grow even when only a few short messages appear. Reading a long report adds its text to the reference content; querying data may also produce results that take space.
content.inputsLessonTitle: 1. Why is context larger than the visible chat?
content.inputsPurpose: These sources help AI understand the task and produce an answer.
content.inputsTitle: What does an answer refer to?
content.keepFiles: Organization does not delete files or undo completed actions.
content.limitCost: Models with larger context windows can handle longer conversations, but still have limits. Processing more content usually takes more computation, costs more and may slow answers and tasks. Long tasks still need organization; no model can retain unlimited context.
content.limitDescription: AI has a limit on how much content it can refer to at once. As the conversation, materials and tool results grow, less space remains. Near the limit, the system automatically summarizes earlier content to make room.
content.limitTitle: 1. Why can’t the entire conversation stay available forever?
content.manualDescription: It lets you request organization earlier and is optional. Even if you never click it, the system organizes when needed. This button does not switch automatic organization on or off.
content.manualOptional: “Organize now” is an optional way to organize earlier. The system also handles it automatically if you never click it.
content.manualTopic: Continue the current topic while the task is unfinished. For a completely different task, create a new topic and provide the necessary background. There is no need to repeatedly organize or start topics just to lower the usage number.
content.memoryDescription: Automatic organization mainly helps you continue the current task. It does not store the entire chat as permanent memory. Tell AI which important preferences or background to save for future use, and read the long-term memory guide.
content.memoryExample: For example, “This report still needs conclusions” is current progress. “I prefer reports to start with conclusions, then supporting evidence” may be a lasting preference. Keep exact numbers and materials you need to quote in original files.
content.memoryTitle: 6. Will future tasks remember this content too?
content.nearLimitDescription: The system automatically organizes earlier content to make room for the rest of the conversation.
content.nearLimitTitle: No action is needed near the limit
content.numbersColors: Colors show an approximate text composition within the used area, not each category’s exact share of capacity. Character estimates cannot precisely split images or audio. Total usage still comes from the model; these estimates are not billing figures.
content.numbersDifference: In the example, the model reports 122K total usage, while input text estimates add up to about 120K. They need not match: totals and text categories use different methods, and the model applies its own counting rules. “About” and “≈” indicate estimates.
content.numbersInputMeaning: Approximately how many tokens does each text category use? For example, 12K of skill instructions and 24K of MCP output.
content.numbersThresholdMeaning: What usage level guides the system’s organization? It comes from the current session configuration rather than a fixed frontend percentage.
content.numbersTitle: 3. How do total usage, estimates and the threshold fit together?
content.numbersUsageMeaning: How much of the capacity has been used? For example, 122K / 200K = 61%.
content.recover: A summary may omit details. AI can look up earlier chats when needed and reread original materials to check exact data.
content.recoverTitle: Missing details can be found in history
content.recoveryHistory: AI can also actively search saved chat history to recover earlier requirements, discussions and conclusions. If a detail is missing from the summary, you do not necessarily have to explain it again. AI can find and read relevant records before continuing.
content.recoverySummary: Organization tries to keep your goal, important requirements, agreed conclusions and unfinished work so AI can continue. Earlier discussions are shortened, so some wording, numbers and details may no longer be complete.
content.recoveryTitle: 2. What if the summary leaves out details?
content.recoveryTradeoff: This is the tradeoff: a summary takes less space but cannot preserve every detail of the original. Automatic organization helps a long task continue; it does not let AI remember an unlimited conversation.
content.reportContinue: You have agreed to analyze by region and already created the table. After organization, you can say “Continue with the main conclusions” without summarizing the whole chat yourself.
content.reportHistory: If AI is unsure about the earlier grouping requirement, it can check chat history. You can also say “Look up the grouping method we agreed on, then continue.” You do not need to paste the entire conversation again.
content.reportOriginal: For an exact number or quote from the report, say “Please reread the report and check this item.” Reading the original material is more reliable than recalling it from a summary.
content.reportTitle: For example, you are writing a report with AI
content.sourcesExampleInstalled: A skill that is installed but not loaded does not contribute its whole file. If its name and description appear in the current skill catalog, that small amount of text still takes space.
content.sourcesExampleOutput: MCP returns 1,000 records, but the script prints a summary of only 10. The summary takes context space, not all 1,000 records.
content.sourcesMcp: MCP connects external tools and services. “MCP output” estimates output with a known source that is actually passed to AI. A script may retrieve a large dataset, then print a small filtered result. Intermediate data that does not enter context is not counted.
content.sourcesMixed: Some scripts combine MCP, file reading and other operations into one output. To avoid guessing, mixed output counts as “Other tools”. A zero MCP estimate therefore does not prove that no MCP calls occurred.
content.sourcesOther: Other tools include ordinary file reads and tool results. Tool definitions are descriptions and parameters directly supplied to AI. A subagent’s entire separate history is not added to the main conversation; only the result it actually returns contributes to the main context.
content.sourcesSkills: Skills provide methods, steps and instructions. Skill catalogs, preloaded content and skill instructions actually read by AI count as “Skill instructions”. The same text is not also counted as system instructions or other tools. Installed skills and content loaded for this request are different things.
content.sourcesTitle: 4. What do the skill and MCP numbers include?
content.summaryContinue: Make room and continue the task
content.summaryTitle: The system creates a summary automatically
content.tokenDescription: Text, images and other content use space according to the model’s rules. Usage is not a message count.
content.tokensLessonDescription: A token is a unit the model uses to measure content, roughly a small piece of text. It is not a fixed one-to-one match with characters or words. Language, code, formatting and the model all affect the count.
content.tokensLessonK: K means thousand. For example, 122K is about 122,000 tokens. Images and other non-text content may also use model space, so counting visible characters is not enough.
content.tokensLessonReading: You do not need to convert each sentence into tokens yourself. Read total usage, capacity and the automatic organization explanation to understand the conversation’s available space.
content.tokensLessonTitle: 2. What is a token, and what does K mean?
content.updatesBreakdown: Categories follow content still referenced in the current request. They do not accumulate every past file read or tool call. When earlier tool results become a task summary, that summary counts as conversation content, without retaining the earlier category numbers.
content.updatesRemaining: The system still keeps important task information and some conversation. Reading new materials also uses space again. Organization does not reset usage to zero or guarantee the same percentage every time.
content.updatesTiming: The card shows the latest usage reported by the model. Organization, the next request using new context, and the model returning updated usage happen at different times.
content.updatesTitle: 6. Why doesn’t usage drop immediately after organization?
content.usageIntro: Context is the content AI refers to for this answer. Higher usage means less space remains.
content.waitingDescription: No extra action is needed. The system prepares the summary automatically, and you can usually continue the task. If it needs time to finish, the task may pause briefly. Wait instead of clicking the button repeatedly to make room.
content.waitingThreshold: The “Automatic organization” marker is a reference for when the system handles usage. Preparation may start earlier rather than exactly at that number. You do not need to monitor the percentage or worry about forgetting to click “Organize now”.
content.waitingTitle: 4. What do I need to do during organization?
content.waitingUsage: Updated usage may appear only after the next answer finishes. A number that does not drop immediately does not by itself mean organization failed.

warningCard.undoMessageContentTip: The content has been revoked, and new messages will not be retained after sending, you can also choose to cancel the operation of this undo.
